notes.meaning: People know how to find veins of silver in the ground and how to refine gold with heat. Humans have great skill in searching out and purifying precious metals buried deep in the earth.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe this chapter is an interlude spoken by the narrator of the book rather than by Job himself.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars view this chapter as a poem inserted by the book's narrator rather than a speech by Job, serving as an interlude on the limits of human wisdom.

notes.meaning: Men dig iron out of the soil and melt copper out of rocks. These useful metals take heavy labor and hot furnaces to separate from raw stone.
Miners carry lamps down into pitch-black depths, putting an end to underground darkness. They push into the farthest and gloomiest spaces to uncover hidden ore.
Workers sink mine shafts far away from where ordinary people live. They dangle on ropes and swing back and forth in deep caverns, forgotten by travelers walking above.
The surface of the earth produces grain that gives bread to eat. Yet deep below that peaceful ground, miners tear through the earth as if it were wrecked by fire.
The underground rocks hold beautiful blue sapphires and flecks of pure gold dust. People take great risks in deep pits because such rich treasures lie hidden there.
No bird of prey knows the dark path down into the mines. Even a falcon with its keen eyesight has never spotted these underground shafts.
Fierce and proud animals like lions have never set foot on these hidden trails. Human miners dare to go into places where the wildest beasts would never venture.
The miner swings his tools against hard flint rock and chips it away. He digs through the very foundations of mountains to uncover what is inside.
Workers cut channels through the solid rock to drain water out of the mine. As the tunnels open up, the miner is able to spot every kind of buried treasure.
The miner dams up underground streams so they cannot leak or seep into the tunnel. By stopping the rushing water, he brings secret treasures out into the light of day.
Job turns from human skill in mining to ask where true wisdom can be found. Men can locate metals deep in the earth, but they cannot dig up the wisdom that understands God's ways.
Human beings do not know the real worth of wisdom. It cannot be found anywhere among mortal men on the surface of the earth.
The deep caverns declare that wisdom is not inside them, and the vast sea says it is not there either. No place in the natural world can produce this heavenly understanding.
Wisdom cannot be bought with the finest gold, nor can its price be weighed out in silver. All the money in the world cannot purchase insight into God's plans.
Even the famous gold of Ophir cannot equal the worth of wisdom. Precious stones like onyx and sapphire fall far short of its value.
Clear crystal and costly golden dishes cannot compare with wisdom. No one can trade the finest manufactured treasures to obtain it.
Rare coral and quartz are not even worth mentioning beside wisdom, and its price is far beyond rubies. God values this insight higher than any gem known to man.
The glowing topaz brought from Cush cannot match wisdom, nor can the purest gold pay for it. The rarest wealth of foreign lands is powerless to buy it.
Job repeats the central question of the poem: where does wisdom come from, and where does understanding dwell? Since neither wealth nor nature holds it, human beings must look elsewhere.
Wisdom is hidden from the eyes of every living person. Even birds soaring high above the ground, with their amazing vision, cannot see where it stays.
Death and the realm of the grave say they have only heard a rumor of wisdom. Even the realm of the dead has not seen it directly, showing that no created realm holds the answer.
God alone understands the path to wisdom, and He alone knows its place. Wisdom belongs to His nature and mind, so only He can reveal it.
God sees to the farthest borders of the earth and observes everything under the heavens. Because His knowledge has no limits, nothing in the universe is hidden from Him.
God gave weight and force to the blowing wind, and He carefully measured out the oceans. He created each part of nature in perfect balance and order.
God made a decree to govern the rainfall, and He traced out the path for thunderbolts. Even wild storms follow the exact boundaries He appointed.
When God formed the universe, He looked upon wisdom and established it as His plan. He examined it thoroughly and put it into action across all creation.

God told mankind that the fear of the Lord is true wisdom, and turning away from evil is understanding. Fearing the Lord does not mean being terrified of Him; it means honoring Him with deep respect and obeying Him. We may not understand all of God's hidden plans, but He calls us to trust and follow Him.

differ.view: Baptists often highlight that Job's words showed his friends that true understanding comes from seeking God humbly rather than falsely accusing a suffering believer.
